'''''Atriplex patula''''' ('''spear saltbush'''; '''common orache'''; '''spear orach'''; '''spreading orach'''; {{IPAc-en|ˈ|ɒ|r|ə|tʃ}}<ref>{{cite encyclopedia | encyclopedia=[[Oxford English Dictionary]] third edition |title=orache |url=http://www.oed.com/view/Entry/132134 |access-date=7 December 2018| date=June 2004 |publisher=Oxford University Press}}</ref>) is a [[ruderal]], circumboreal species of [[annual plant|annual]] [[herbaceous plant]] in the genus ''[[Atriplex]]'' naturalized in many temperate regions.

== Description ==
''Atriplex patula'' grows to be between {{Convert|50 and 80|cm|abbr=off}} tall.<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last1=Sukhorukov |first1=Alexander |last2=Kushunina |first2=Maria |last3=Verloove |first3=Filip |date=14 July 2016 |title=Notes on Atriplex, Oxybasis and Dysphania (Chenopodiaceae) in West-Central Tropical Africa |journal=Plant Ecology and Evolution |volume=149 |issue=2 |pages=249–256 |doi=10.5091/plecevo.2016.1181|bibcode=2016PlEcE.149..249S |doi-access=free }}</ref> The branches extend outwards from the stem with [[Glossary of leaf morphology|rhomboid leaves]] and separated clusters of flowers.<ref name=":0" /> The species accumulates salt from the environment in its tissues. Unlike other ''[[Atriplex]]'' species, it lacks notable salt bladders to excrete salt onto the leaves.<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal|last1=Mann|first1=Ellen|last2=Rutter|first2=Allison|last3=Zeeb|first3=Barbara|date=October 2020|title=Evaluating the efficacy of Atriplex spp. in the phytoextraction of road salt (NaCl) from contaminated soil|url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S0269749120310459|journal=Environmental Pollution|language=en|volume=265|issue=Pt B|article-number=114963|doi=10.1016/j.envpol.2020.114963|pmid=32806446|bibcode=2020EPoll.26514963M|s2cid=221162683|url-access=subscription|archive-date=7 October 2021|access-date=16 February 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211007001627/https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S0269749120310459|url-status=live}}</ref>

== Taxonomy ==
The species was a member of the family [[Chenopodiaceae]], now part of Amaranthaceae, the [[amaranth]] family.<ref name=":0" />

== Distribution and habitat ==
The species has a wide range, including semi-arid deserts and coastal areas in [[Asia]], [[North America]], [[Europe]], and [[Africa]].<ref name=":0" /> It commonly grows along roads and waste sites.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Prokopiev |first1=I. A. |last2=Filippova |first2=F. V. |last3=Shein |first3=A. A. |date=March 2012 |title=Effect of anthropogenic pollution with dust containing heavy metals on seed progeny of spear saltbush |url=http://link.springer.com/10.1134/S1021443712020148 |journal=Russian Journal of Plant Physiology |language=en |volume=59 |issue=2 |pages=212–216 |doi=10.1134/S1021443712020148 |bibcode=2012RuJPP..59..212P |issn=1021-4437 |s2cid=17780607|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

Although it is commonly asserted that the species has been naturalized in North America only since the 18th century,<ref>{{eFloras|1|242414718|Atriplex patula|volume=4 |last=Welsh |first=Stanley L.}}</ref><ref>{{PLANTS |symbol=ATPA4 |taxon=USDA PLANTS Profile |access-date=20 May 2008}}</ref> seeds ascribed to this species occur on the west coast of North America in buried marsh deposits that predate [[European colonization of the Americas|European contact]].<ref>Sherrod BL, 2001. Geological Society of America Bulletin 113, 1299–1311.</ref><ref>Milker Y, et al., 2016. Quaternary Science Reviews 142, 143–163.</ref>

== Uses ==
The young leaves and shoots are edible raw or cooked and suffice as a [[spinach]] substitute,<ref>{{cite book |last=Mabey |first=Richard |title=Food for Free |publisher=Collins |year=2012 |isbn=978-000-743847-1 |location=London |page=104 |author-link=Richard Mabey}}</ref> but are bland on their own.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Francis-Baker |first=Tiffany |title=Concise Foraging Guide |date=2021 |publisher=[[Bloomsbury Publishing|Bloomsbury]] |isbn=978-1-4729-8474-6 |series=[[The Wildlife Trusts]] |location=London |page=54}}</ref>

The species has been proven to be effective in lowering salt content in soils when planted in areas with high road salt contamination.<ref name=":1" />
